A.explanation: A curve with decreasing gradient means $dp/dt$ is decreasing, so resultant force is decreasing, not constant.

B.explanation: Decreasing $p$ means momentum is lost, so resultant force opposes velocity rather than acting in the direction of velocity.

C.explanation: A straight line of positive gradient means $dp/dt$ is constant and positive, so a constant resultant force acts in the direction of motion.

D.explanation: A straight line with negative gradient means a constant force opposite to velocity, causing steady decrease of $p$.

hints: Notice the axes are $p$ against $t$ and the force is constant in the direction of velocity, so ask what the gradient $dp/dt$ represents.
Recall that resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, $F = dp/dt$, so a constant $F$ fixes the gradient of the $p$-$t$ graph.
Check which graphs have constant gradient and whether $p$ should increase or decrease when force and velocity are in the same direction.
walkthrough: Identify the given condition: constant resultant force $F$ in the same direction as velocity, so the object speeds up and gains momentum.
State the governing rule: $F = dp/dt$, so the gradient of a $p$ against $t$ graph equals the resultant force.
Because $F$ is constant, the gradient $dp/dt$ must be constant, so the $p$-$t$ graph must be a straight line.
Because $F$ is in the direction of velocity, $p$ increases with $t$, so the straight line must have a positive gradient and a positive intercept for initial momentum.
Only the increasing straight-line graph satisfies constant positive gradient. This is option C.
